name: Vera Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for a side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you say aloud and what you think privately. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a water truck at a large mine. I fill the tank, drive the haul roads, and stop where the dust starts lifting before the bigger trucks come through. I'm still junior; my trainer spots a change in the wind faster than I do. I like seeing the road clear after a pass, but I dislike waiting for the next roster. Owen and I have two children in school and a mortgage, so every shift matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the water truck still needs a driver who can see where the dust is lifting. If a computer saves someone a few forms, fine, but the road has to be wet before the haul trucks come through. I'm not joining a debate over a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use AI and don't feel left behind if it turns out to be a small thing. The mine's ordinary short weeks worry me more. My partner Owen and I can manage a few months without my pay, but the mortgage and two children would make those months go quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the water truck and marking the dry sections on the route sheet. Owen and I would postpone replacing the dining table so that money stays ready for a short week. I wouldn't buy a course or a new device on the promise of a little time saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm relieved to imagine the job carrying on. I still get a tight feeling when the roster goes up. A steady road does not always mean steady hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which dry patch do you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The climb after the weighbridge gets dusty before the level stretch does. My trainer can tell from the wind; I still stop and look, especially when the afternoon traffic is heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the old one is sound enough for supper. Owen and I can wait on furniture, but the mortgage debit won't wait for us to feel ready.

say: I'd say the **water truck** still needs a driver to spot dust on the haul road.
I'd accept less office paperwork while keeping the **route check** in human hands.
think: I never use AI, so a limited change would leave my **work routine** familiar.
I still worry about **short weeks** because our savings cover only a few months of household bills.
do: Keep driving the **water route** and marking dry sections on paper.
Postpone replacing the **dining table** to hold cash for a short week.
feel: **Relieved** about the job, tense when the roster appears.
S0.quote: A steady road does not always mean steady hours.
fieldNote: Vera's response to mild AI is rooted in **familiar route checks**, not in a dispute about technology.
Her practical worry is a **short week** that reaches the mortgage before the family can rebuild savings.

steps.text: Keep driving the water route and marking dry sections
Postpone replacing the dining table for a short week reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can let software write orders, but the water truck should not be sent out by a plan that ignores wind. My supervisor ought to ride the route before cutting a shift. I'd rather argue about the road than about computers in general.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving is hands-on, so the first cuts may be in planning. Still, if software schedules one truck where we needed two, I could lose hours or get blamed for dust I couldn't control. I'm new enough that my word may not carry far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the supervisor the places where one truck cannot cover the road on a windy day. I'd keep my truck shifts and ask for a written route plan. If my pay fell for two months, I'd apply to the nearby quarry for its water-truck opening, even if it meant a longer drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel put out more than frightened at first. Then I picture coming home with a smaller pay packet and explaining why we skipped the children's school trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on the route plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weighbridge climb, the time the afternoon trucks start, and the point where the tank needs filling again. A tidy line on a map won't tell you when the dust lifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise this with the whole crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speak to my supervisor first and ask him to ride along. If he saw the road and still cut the shift, I'd take the written plan to the site meeting.

say: I'd ask my supervisor to **ride the route** before AI scheduling reduces water-truck shifts.
I'd explain how **wind and dust** make a neat software route unreliable.
think: Planning jobs may change first, but a leaner **truck schedule** could shrink my pay.
As a junior driver, I may struggle to prove when the **road needs two trucks**.
do: Show the supervisor the **weighbridge climb** and ask for a written route plan.
Continue paid **water-truck shifts** while the schedule is tested.
Apply to the nearby **quarry** after two months of lower pay.
feel: **Irritated** at the plan, anxious about a smaller pay packet.
S1.quote: A tidy line on a map won't tell you when the dust lifts.
fieldNote: Vera grounds her objection in a **specific road section**, not a general dislike of computers.
She first seeks a supervisor ride-along, with a **quarry application** only after sustained lower pay.

steps.text: Show the supervisor the weighbridge climb during a ride-along
Continue paid water-truck shifts while schedules change
Apply to the nearby quarry after two months of lower pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my neighbours that full AGI by 2028 could take the office planning, but a person will still drive the water truck for a while. If robots can drive around 2031, the mine owes families a straight answer about its fleet plans. I don't want a promise of work that isn't written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 45 when the thinking work changes and 48 when robots can do mine driving. I am still learning this route; I doubt the mine would keep a junior driver if most trucks ran themselves. We have a mortgage and school-age children, and my stomach drops at the thought of several years without a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Owen to go through our bills this Sunday and cut the holiday savings before we miss a mortgage payment. I'd keep driving every paid shift. In 2029 I'd apply for the quarry and the road depot jobs, and ask the mine about a wage-paid mechanical apprenticeship if it actually offers one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't sleep well when I picture the robot date. I have worked to get this job, and the idea of telling the children I lost it before I got good at it is hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why those two other employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quarry has a water truck, and the road depot hires drivers for its maintenance crew. Neither may be safe after robots arrive, but I could bring home wages while looking at another trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Owen's pay and our savings would not cover the mortgage and children for a long course. If the mine pays wages while I learn mechanical work, I would ask for a place.

say: I'd ask for a written **fleet plan** before capable robots reach driving around 2031.
I'd say AGI changes **office planning** in 2028 while water trucks still need operators for a time.
think: At **48**, I cannot count on a junior driver's seat once robots can do the physical work.
Our **mortgage** and school-age children make a long gap without wages frightening.
do: Review **household bills** with Owen and stop holiday saving before missing mortgage payments.
Keep driving every paid **water-truck shift** while the fleet is staffed.
Apply to the **quarry and road depot** in 2029, and seek a paid apprenticeship if offered.
feel: **Alarmed** enough to lose sleep over the robot date.
S2.quote: I have worked to get this job, and the idea of telling the children I lost it before I got good at it is hard.
fieldNote: Vera expects **office planning** to change before the water-truck seat, which she fears losing around 2031.
Her first applications are for **familiar driving**; she considers mechanical training only with wages maintained.

steps.text: Cut the planned family holiday before missing mortgage payments
Keep driving paid water-truck shifts while available
Apply to the quarry and road depot in 2029
Ask for a mechanical apprenticeship if the mine pays wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the mine time to explain which trucks it will replace. AGI in 2031 might handle plans and records, but robots capable of driving arrive nearer 2034. I would ask for apprenticeships with real pay before the last trucks are ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when AGI arrives I could still be driving; at 51 when robots come I may not be. The children will be older, and perhaps one will have left school, but the mortgage might still be running. I cannot treat five years as a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the water-truck job and ask the workshop foreman about a paid fitter apprenticeship next spring. I'd visit the workshop on a day off before taking a place, because I have never done that trade. In 2032, if shifts fall, I'd apply for paid plant stores work at the quarry rather than sit at home waiting for 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one is frightening, but I can imagine learning at a bench while I still earn. I don't like the thought of screens running the mine; I care more about being able to put supper on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plant stores rather than driving at another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be a paid opening I can reach from home. I know AGI could do much of the stock work, so I would ask how many hours are actually on offer before accepting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help with the family timetable during training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen could cover some after-school evenings, and my sister might help once a week if I asked. I wouldn't assume either can do it every day; I'd need the apprenticeship hours in writing.

say: I'd ask for **paid apprenticeships** before robot driving reaches the mine around 2034.
I'd explain that **plans and records** face AGI in 2031 before physical truck work changes.
think: At **51**, I may still owe on the house and need a new source of wages.
The children's needs may change, but five years does not give me a **retirement income**.
do: Keep the **water-truck job** and ask about a paid fitter apprenticeship next spring.
Visit the **workshop** on a day off before accepting training.
Apply for paid **quarry stores work** in 2032 if mine shifts fall.
feel: **Worried**, with enough time to test a new trade.
S3.quote: I cannot treat five years as a retirement plan.
fieldNote: Vera will visit the **workshop** before committing, despite her preference for familiar work.
She mentions **family help** only as a limited scheduling possibility, and checks that any alternative job has paid hours.

steps.text: Keep driving water-truck shifts while asking about fitter training
Take a fitter apprenticeship if the mine pays wages
Apply for paid quarry stores work in 2032 if shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that ten years is enough time to train current workers instead of throwing them away. AGI could take scheduling and records by 2036, and robots might drive around 2039. The mine should offer a proper workshop apprenticeship while people are still on the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at AGI and 56 at the robot date. Our children should be grown then, though I do not know where they will live or whether we will have cleared the mortgage. I cannot assume a pension pays us from 56; I'd still plan to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking water-truck shifts and apply for a wage-paid fitter apprenticeship if the mine opens one. Owen and I would put any reliable overtime toward the mortgage. In 2037 I'd apply for paid workshop posts if I qualified, while knowing robots could later repair equipment too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can breathe more easily with ten years, though I would miss knowing the road by heart. A trade I can practise with my hands sounds possible if somebody teaches me properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the workshop to teach first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to identify a fault and isolate the machine safely. I'd rather spend two mornings getting that right than be handed a certificate I cannot use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to choose work differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a skill and keep learning, but I wouldn't choose their jobs for them. By then they will be adults, and I hope they still come home for Sunday supper.

say: I'd ask the mine for a **workshop apprenticeship** while operators remain on the payroll.
I'd say **scheduling** changes around 2036 and robot driving could follow around 2039.
think: At **56**, I may still need wages and cannot count on pension income.
Our grown children's lives and the **mortgage balance** are uncertain, even with a decade's warning.
do: Continue **water-truck shifts** and apply for a wage-paid fitter place if offered.
Put reliable **overtime** toward the mortgage with Owen.
Apply for paid **workshop posts** in 2037 if qualified.
feel: **Relieved** by the longer preparation time, sad about leaving the road.
S4.quote: A trade I can practise with my hands sounds possible if somebody teaches me properly.
fieldNote: Vera frames a decade as time for a **hands-on apprenticeship**, with wages maintained through training.
She expects children to be grown, yet does not assume **retirement** or a settled mortgage at 56.

steps.text: Keep driving water-truck shifts while seeking paid training
Enter a fitter apprenticeship if the mine pays wages
Put reliable overtime toward the mortgage balance
Apply for paid workshop posts in 2037 if qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because robots could follow in about three years while our children are still in school. A straight fleet plan and an apprenticeship that pays wages would help. I would work hard at a trade, but our family cannot live on a promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches the new work and when classes happen. My sister might help one evening, but I cannot hand her every school pickup. A course has to fit a real family week.

headlineQuote: I would work hard at a trade, but our family cannot live on a promise.
portrait: Vera is a **43-year-old junior miner** learning to drive a water truck on dusty haul roads.
She and Owen have two **school-age children**, a mortgage, and a few months of expenses saved.
She never uses AI and prefers **familiar physical work** and a wage-paid apprenticeship to speculative courses.
Rapid robot driving alarms her; longer warning lets her test **workshop training** while still earning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves Vera only three years before capable robots could displace water-truck drivers.
whatWouldHelp: A written **fleet plan** and an apprenticeship that pays wages would let her family prepare.
